chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated it as a disconnected chain (mursal), saying: Some of our companions said its chain of narration was lost from me, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him).

He said: 'Indeed, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, did not leave anything that is needed without teaching it to His Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). Among His teaching to him was that he ascended the pulpit one day, praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: O people, Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to me from the Subtle, the Knowing, and said: Indeed, virgins are like fruit on a tree; when their fruit ripens and is not picked, the sun spoils it and the winds scatter it. And so are virgins; when they reach what women reach, they have no remedy except marriage, otherwise corruption is not guaranteed against them because they are human.'

He said: A man stood up to him and said: O Messenger of Allah, whom should I marry? He said: 'The equals.' He said: O Messenger of Allah, who are the equals? He said: 'The believers are equals of one another.'
And it is disliked to marry a drinker of wine, even though it is not forbidden. Narrated.

key_terms.مُرْسَلًا: Disconnected chain (where a tabi'i narrates directly from a companion without an intermediate link)

ai.seo_question: What is the jurisprudential ruling and wisdom regarding marriage for virgins in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* underscores the naturalistic wisdom of marriage in Shia jurisprudence, framing it as a necessary outlet for human desire to prevent moral decay, particularly for virgins. It establishes the egalitarian principle that 'believers are equals of one another' (*al-mu'minuna ba'duhum akfa'u ba'd*), prioritizing piety over lineage or wealth, while also noting the recommended dislike (*karahah*) of marrying those who consume wine despite its permissibility.
